Languages

A familiar greeting can open a door that gold cannot. An inscription can preserve an enemy's warning long after the enemy is dust. Languages tell you whom your hero can understand and which voices shaped their life. They do not determine ancestry, allegiance or character.

Choose your languages

Begin with Common and one other ordinary language learned in the community that raised you. Common is the campaign's shared trade language; the DA may give it a local name. Choose your other language with the DA from the list below or the campaign's equivalent. Any ancestry may know any language. Culture suggests where you learned it, rather than imposing a compulsory choice.

Record the language's actual name, not just “regional” or “community language.” If Common was your only home language, choose another ordinary language learned through neighbors, work or travel. This starting choice is separate from your culture's discipline and ability pair and costs no DP.

Apply explicit extra grants afterward. A Foot in Two Worlds grants two additional ordinary spoken languages. Choose two distinct languages you do not already know; it does not grant another culture's abilities. A signed language is an ordinary language when the campaign uses it, but a grant restricted to spoken languages does not include it.

Unless a grant says otherwise, knowing a language includes speaking, understanding, and reading and writing its usual script, if it has one. A grant that specifically says spoken, understands or cannot speak keeps that restriction. Record such limits beside the language. Speaking a language does not require a separate skill rating, and attributes grant no automatic extra languages.

Ordinary languages

These are starting options, not a required history of the world. Their names describe familiar traditions; anyone raised among their speakers may learn them. Each row is one language unless it explicitly asks you to name a particular one.

LanguageWhere you might learn or encounter it
CommonMarkets, mixed settlements, roads and adventuring companies.
Regional languageChoose one named local language: a river kingdom, island community or frontier valley. Each is a separate choice.
DwarvenDeep halls, quarry towns and craft communities; records of lineage, work and agreements.
ElvenWoodland settlements and long-lived artistic traditions; songs, histories and correspondence.
HalflingHearth communities, traveling families and river villages; stories and everyday business.
GoblinGoblin communities and their neighbors; salvage yards, markets and warrens.
OrcOrc communities and their neighbors; border settlements, expeditions and oral histories.
GiantGiant communities and peoples who trade with them; landmarks, stone records and remembered journeys.
KoboldKobold communities and their neighbors; tunnel works, workshops and trading posts.
Harbor CantMultilingual ports and ship crews. A full local language, not universal knowledge of every sailor's slang.
Way SignA complete signed language shared by participating communities. Communication requires sight and usable signing gestures.

Uncommon and ancient languages

These languages are not included in an unrestricted ordinary language grant. Choose one only when a grant explicitly allows it or the DA makes it an ordinary option for the campaign before character creation. Their availability reflects the setting, not a higher numerical bonus.

LanguageWhere it becomes useful
DraconicSpeaking with dragons and their learned allies; reading draconic inscriptions. Kobold is a separate language.
FeyNegotiating with fey courts and woodland powers; understanding their stories and spoken bargains.
InfernalSpeaking with fiends and interpreting their correspondence or contracts. Knowing it does not bind or summon anything.
CelestialConversations with celestial beings and some sacred traditions. It grants no divine authority.
ElementalSpeech used by elemental beings capable of language. It does not let you command fire, weather or an unintelligent elemental.
Elder TongueChoose one named lost or ancient scholarly language. Different vanished civilizations need not share it.

A sacred text may be written in Common, Dwarven or any other language. “Sacred,” “scholarly” and “courtly” describe use, not automatic additional languages. Beasts' calls, a spirit's images and a construct's signal lights are forms of communication, not languages you gain by choosing a row in these tables.

Use languages at the table

When you share a language and can hear, see or read it as required, ordinary communication needs no roll. State what you say or ask. A conversation can still involve uncertainty about persuasion, deception or evidence; use the normal attribute or the ability you declared. Knowing the words does not make the listener agree, reveal secrets or recognize your authority.

A language barrier is not simply extra Banes on a roll. Without a shared means of communication, you cannot deliver a precise argument merely by rolling well. Pointing, drawing or demonstrating can convey something simple: “danger there,” “follow me,” or an offered trade. Agree on what is actually understood. An interpreter, a translation, or an applicable ability can make a more complicated exchange possible. A card that explicitly requires a shared language still requires one; an interpreter does not silently change its target requirement.

Reading a clear message in a language you can read needs no roll. Damaged text, an unfamiliar technical subject or a cipher may present a separate problem. Sharing an alphabet does not grant another language, and a cipher is not an extra language choice. Ask the DA what evidence or expertise could make progress possible.

Translate the Fragment supplies a way to interpret unfamiliar written text. Use its printed time, progress and outcomes. Completing a translation does not teach you the whole language. A copied voice or disguise likewise supplies no vocabulary or memories unless its ability explicitly says so.

Learn another language

@UUID[Compendium.heroes-of-legend.player-rules.JournalEntry.7dde82adde18027d.JournalEntryPage.b2ef1858c60e2bb9]{Another Tongue} costs 1 DP and grants one additional ordinary language, including its usual script if it has one. It requires no discipline and may be purchased once, during level-0 creation or later. Record the language you choose. This is a specific card grant, not a repeatable price for buying every language or permission to learn a secret language.

Keep learning grounded

Record new languages when an explicit trait, ability or agreed campaign grant provides them. Time with a teacher, a community or useful texts explains that learning; it does not create an unstated free advancement or a new universal DP price. Agree on the route before spending time or DP. Translation and ordinary practice remain useful even when they do not grant permanent fluency.

> At the gate. An elf raised in a dwarven mining town chooses Common and > Dwarven. She reads the quarry's warning without a roll. Its damaged diagram > still needs investigation. Her human companion's extra spoken Goblin lets him > question a salvager, but does not let him read the salvager's written ledger.
